newsitem.title: UK: Britain, Germany improve position on EU grains mkt.
newsitem.headline: Britain, Germany improve position on EU grains mkt.

text.p: Britain and Germany have improved their position on Europe's domestic grain market, with the help of a stand-off on France's market and, in Britain's case, by currency moves.
French wheat prices were steady early this week with buyers and sellers engaged in a war of nerves, dealers said.
But prices firmed on Thursday after exporters bid via France to export over one million tonnes of wheat at prices traders described as "very aggressive" at the latest EU grain tender.
Barley and maize were broadly unchanged over the previous week as there was little fresh news to drive prices.
Faced with sellers determined to hold on to firm prices, wheat buyers have tried to delay cover despite a heavy loading schedule in ports, they said.
But on Thursday prompt wheat into Rouen was bid at 890 per tonne and offered at 895 francs per tonne, up five francs on Wednesday.
"The bids came as a surprise to the French market," one trader said, adding sellers were now bound to remain on the sidelines.
In France exporters bid to export 1,097,500 tonnes of free-market soft wheat at subsidies ranging from 8.73 to 17.99 Ecus per tonne, national grain office ONIC reported.
The best bid of 8.73 Ecus per tonne meant a world price of around $161 per tonne, Fob April, and was for the export of up to 125,000 tonnes of wheat, exporters said.
Wheat volume bid in France was hefty but traders noted there would be no grain tenders next Thursday for Easter.
Last week the EU's grain panel granted licences for the export of 273,500 tonnes of free-market soft wheat at a maximum rebate of 11.47 Ecus per tonne.
On the export front Algeria has launched a tender for the export of 75,000 tonnes of optional-origin milling wheat.
But French exporters said they had been excluded from the tender in what they described as possible evidence of new political tensions between France and Algeria.
Traders said French wheat could still be sold in the tender but only through non-French companies or foreign subsidiaries of French firms.
Barley prices were quoted at 850 francs per tonne on Thursday as traders still await confirmation Saudi Arabia may soon be back in the market for feed-barley.
A report Saudi Arabia was tendering on April 1 for a million tonnes was widely discounted.
UK grains are competitive again, thanks to a lower sterling, British traders said.
The fall in sterling was largely responsible for a 1.45 stg jump in the bellwether May wheat contract at LIFFE, traders said.
Although the UK grain market has tightened up, there are still exports needed, traders said. They hoped the easier pound would last long enough to give them a good window of export opportunity.
"There are still exports required," one trader said. "Obviously it's a bit tighter than it was," he said.
He reckoned compounder demand for grain was still healthy, but feed industry sources felt that the industry was fairly well bought forward.
"The consumer part of the market is reasonably well covered," one industrial consumer buyer said.
Consumers had covered themselves steadily over the past few months, despite limited supplies off farms.

"There's no doubt there's quite a bit left to do, but its the last ten per cent," he said. Feed compounders, millers and industrial users were congratulating themselves on having largely avoided the most recent price rises.
And with little left to buy, they would not worry too much about having to get the last of their supplies in a rising market.
"I haven't heard any reports of consumers desperate to buy for weeks," he said.

German traders reckon they have the cheapest market in Europe. "We're importing nothing but old contracts," one said. And traders were buying back deals for imported wheat to replace it with domestic production.
The trader reckoned that most of the EU's barley exports through Rotterdam and other northern ports were coming from Germany.
Spanish feed and milling wheat ex-farm prices pushed higher as the prospect of crop damage loomed due to a lack of rain.
Farmers say water has been scarce and is much-needed. Without rain, this year's crop could suffer and there are already signs of some damage in the south, traders said.
However, this scarcely affected durum wheat prices with little trading taking place.
Barley prices were largely unchanged, but traders said farmers were complaining that they needed more water for their crops.
Wheat prices were marginally higher. Demand for April or May delivery remained high with prices around 23,500.
Italian wheat prices were slightly higher this week as foreign wheat price increases continued to be magnified by the weakening of the lira over the past week.
